## How Trees Grow Equally in All Directions

## 1. The Essential Problem:

The main question is: **How do trees manage to grow equally in all directions, even in the absence of uniform sunlight availability?** This seems counterintuitive, especially when potted plants clearly grow towards the light.

## 2. Step-by-Step Reasoning:

Here's how we can break down the problem and approach a possible answer:

**a) Understanding Growth Mechanisms:**

- Trees primarily grow upwards due to a specialized tissue called the **apical meristem** located at the tip of the shoot. This meristem contains actively dividing cells that contribute to the elongation of the stem.
- **Lateral buds** along the stem also contribute to growth by forming branches.

**b) Sunlight and Growth:**

- While sunlight is crucial for photosynthesis (the process by which plants create food), it doesn't directly control the direction of growth in all cases.
- The apical meristem and lateral buds have an inherent capacity for **gravitropism** (response to gravity) and **thigmotropism** (response to touch). This means they can sense their orientation and adjust growth accordingly.
- In most cases, the main stem grows vertically due to positive gravitropism, while branches exhibit negative gravitropism, growing outwards and upwards.

**c) Tree Architecture and Sunlight Distribution:**

- Trees have evolved complex mechanisms to optimize light capture. Their branches often grow in a spiral pattern, allowing for even distribution of leaves across the canopy.
- This branching pattern minimizes self-shading and ensures that leaves on all sides have access to sunlight.

**d) Compensatory Growth in Response to Uneven Light:**

- While trees strive for balanced growth, they can exhibit compensatory mechanisms when exposed to uneven light conditions.
- If one side of the tree receives less sunlight, the growth rate on that side might be slightly slower compared to the sunlit side. However, trees can adjust their growth patterns over time to maintain a balanced structure.
- This involves increased growth on the shaded side and/or reduced growth on the sunlit side, leading to a more symmetrical overall shape.

**e) Role of Hormones in Growth Regulation:**

- Plant hormones play a critical role in regulating growth and development. Auxin, a key hormone, is involved in phototropism (response to light).
- In trees, auxin tends to accumulate on the shaded side of the stem, promoting cell elongation and growth in that direction. This helps compensate for the reduced light exposure.

## 3. Draft Answer:

Trees achieve balanced growth through a combination of factors:

- Inherent growth patterns guided by gravitropism and thigmotropism.
- Efficient branching patterns for optimal light capture.
- Compensatory growth mechanisms in response to uneven light distribution.
- Hormonal regulation, particularly by auxin, which promotes growth on the shaded side.

While sunlight is essential for plant growth, trees prioritize balanced architecture over simply growing towards the light. This allows them to optimize resource utilization and maintain structural stability, even in environments with uneven light conditions. 

It's important to note that this is a simplified explanation, and the actual mechanisms controlling tree growth are complex and involve multiple interacting factors. Further research is still ongoing to fully understand the intricate details of this fascinating process.
gold_answer:
$\begingroup$

There are some other good answers which provide part of the picture, but I
think there is a fundamental organising principle which has been missed.
Konrad has touched on it in his answer.

**The reason trees, and most plants, tend to grow equally in all directions is
that they have iteratively generated branching and radial symmetry which is
controlled in a feedback loop of the growth promoting hormone auxin and auxin-
sensitive auxin transporters. This is an elegant biological algorithm which
explains all branching growth.**

The things Konrad identifies (phototropism, gravitropism, etc.) serve as
orientation cues which help the plant determine which axes to grow along, but
fundamentally the process is about auxin gradients. There are exceptions, as
others have pointed out in their answers, and they usually result from severe
imbalances in the orientation cues.

I'll try to explain the growth process clearly (and it gives me an opportunity
to try my hand at diagramming again ^_^)...

* * *

Auxin is a plant hormone (actually a class of hormones, but mostly when people
say auxin, they mean [ indole-3-acetic acid
](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indole-3-acetic_acid) ) which promotes cell
elongation and division. The basic principle which allows auxin to act in the
organising way it does is that auxin is produced inside cells, and proteins
which export auxin from a cell develop on the side of the cell which has the
highest auxin concentration (see figure below).

![cells export auxin more on the side which has the highest auxin
concentration](https://i.sstatic.net/VGbXI.png)

**So auxin gets transported up the concentration gradient of auxin!** Thus if
you get an area of high auxin concentration developing somehow, more auxin is
then transported towards that area. An area of high auxin concentration
relative to the surrounding tissue is called an **auxin maximum** (plural
'maxima').

For most of the life of the plant, auxin is produced pretty much equally in
most cells. However, at the very early stages of embryo development, it gets
produced preferentially along the embryonic axis (see figure below, **part 1**
). That creates a **meristem** \- a group of cells where cell division is
taking place - at the auxin maximum at each end of the embryo. Since this
particular meristem is at the apex of the plant, it is called the **apical
meristem** , and it is usually the strongest one in the plant.

![auxin patterning of plant growth](https://i.sstatic.net/bSY6i.png)

So by having a meristem at each end, the embryo then elongates as cell
division is only taking place at those points. This leads to **part 2** of the
image above, where the two meristems get so far apart that the auxin gradient
is so weak as to no longer have its organising effect (area in the red
square). When that happens, the auxin produced in cells in that area
concentrates in a chaotic way for a short time until another center of
transport is created. This happens, as the first one did, when a particular
area of the tissue has a slightly higher concentration of auxin, and so auxin
in the surrounding tissue is transported towards it. This leads to **part 3**
of the figure, in which two new meristems are created on the sides of the
plant (called **lateral meristems** ).

Lateral meristems are where branches occur on plants. If you then imagine this
process continuing to iterate over and over, you will see that the branches,
as they elongate, will develop meristems at the tips and along the sides. The
main stem will also continue elongating, and develop more lateral stems. The
root will begin to branch, and those branches will branch, etc. If you can
understand how this elegant system works, you understand how plants grow, and
why they grow in repeating units as opposed to in a body plan like animals.

It also explains why, if you cut off the tip of a stem, it promotes branching.
By removing the apical meristem, you get rid of the auxin gradient and enable
the creating of multiple smaller meristems which each develop into branches.

So far I've explained regular branching, but the same system causes the radial
symmetry which makes trees (usually) grow in all directions equally...

![enter image description here](https://i.sstatic.net/81e6B.png)

Imagine taking a cross section through a stem and looking down all the way
through it (as depicted crudely above). Just as auxin gradients act to
coordinate growth along the length of the plant, they also coordinate it
radially, as the maxima will tend to space themselves out as far from one
another as possible. That leads to branches growing in all directions equally
(on average).

I welcome comments on this answer, as I think its so important to
understanding plant growth that I'd like to hone my answer to make it as good
as possible.
